PSA.40.1: Opening a psalm of thanksgiving, David recalls a time he waited patiently for the Lord, who eventually turned and heard his cry.
PSA.41.1: Opening this psalm, David pronounces a blessing on anyone who shows care for the poor, promising the Lord will look after such a person in turn.
PSA.44.26: This communal lament, sung by the sons of Korah after a national defeat, ends with a short, urgent plea for God to rise up and help for the sake of his mercy.
PSA.46.5: Describing a city made secure by God's presence rather than its own defenses, this psalm declares she will not be shaken because God is within her.
PSA.50.15: In a psalm attributed to Asaph where God himself speaks, he tells his people to call on him in trouble, promising deliverance and asking to be honored for it.
PSA.51.12: In this psalm of repentance written after his sin with Bathsheba, David asks God not merely to forgive him but to restore the joy he has lost.
PSA.54.4: Betrayed to Saul by the Ziphites while hiding as a fugitive, David responds to that danger by declaring that God himself is the helper standing with him.
PSA.55.6: Overwhelmed by fear and betrayed by a close friend, David wishes aloud for wings like a dove so he could simply fly away from it all.
PSA.57.1: Written for a time David hid from Saul in a cave, this psalm opens with a plea for mercy and an image of finding refuge under God's wings.
PSA.62.1: Facing enemies who plot against him, David opens this psalm by describing his soul as one that waits quietly, since his salvation comes only from God.
PSA.63.1: Composed while David was in the wilderness of Judah, this psalm opens by comparing his longing for God to a thirst in a dry and waterless land.
PSA.66.20: Closing a psalm about prayer being blocked by unconfessed sin, the speaker blesses God specifically for not turning away his prayer or withholding mercy.
PSA.68.19: In a psalm celebrating God's triumphant march among his people, the writer blesses the Lord for daily carrying the burdens of his people.
PSA.69.30: Near the end of a psalm full of suffering and appeals for rescue, David shifts to promise that he will praise God's name in song once help comes.
PSA.71.3: An older voice in this psalm asks God to be a permanent refuge to return to again and again, calling him rock and fortress.
PSA.71.14: Even while pleading for rescue from enemies, the psalmist commits to keep hoping and to increase his praise rather than despair.
PSA.73.24: After nearly stumbling into envy over the prosperity of the wicked, the psalmist Asaph resolves that God will guide him now and receive him afterward.
PSA.73.28: Concluding his struggle over why evil people seem to prosper, Asaph decides that drawing near to God is simply better than anything else.
PSA.85.6: Praying for national restoration after some past judgment, this psalm asks God to revive his people so that they can rejoice in him again.
PSA.86.11: In a personal prayer for help, David asks God to teach him God's way and to unite his often divided heart around reverence for God's name.
PSA.86.15: Appealing for mercy against violent enemies, David grounds his hope in a description of God's character as compassionate, gracious, and full of mercy and truth.
PSA.94.18: Recalling a moment when he felt himself slipping, the psalmist credits God's steady mercy with holding him up before he fell.
PSA.102.27: Contrasting his own fleeting life with the created order that will eventually wear out, the psalmist marvels that God alone remains unchanged and eternal.
PSA.107.9: In a psalm recounting how God rescues travelers, prisoners, and the sick, this line praises him for satisfying the hungry and thirsty soul.
PSA.107.29: Describing sailors caught in a storm at sea who cry out to God, this verse credits him with calming the storm and stilling the waves.
PSA.117.2: One of the shortest psalms in the collection, this closing line grounds Israel's praise in God's enduring mercy and unfailing truth.
PSA.119.28: In this long acrostic meditation on God's law, the psalmist admits his soul is worn down by grief and asks to be strengthened by God's word.
PSA.119.71: Looking back on a season of suffering, the psalmist concludes that being afflicted actually served him well, since it taught him God's statutes.
PSA.119.76: Still working through this extended psalm on God's word, the writer asks for God's kindness to comfort him just as God had promised his servant.
PSA.119.114: In the midst of praising God's law, the psalmist calls God his hiding place and shield, resting his hope entirely on God's word.
PSA.119.165: Near the close of this long psalm, the writer observes that people who love God's law enjoy a deep peace that nothing can disturb.
PSA.121.8: This pilgrim's psalm of protection ends by promising that the Lord watches over every departure and every return, now and always.
PSA.122.1: Opening a psalm sung by pilgrims traveling up to Jerusalem for worship, David recalls his gladness at the invitation to go to the Lord's house.
PSA.124.8: This short psalm of thanksgiving for a narrow escape from danger ends by locating all real help in the name of the Lord, maker of heaven and earth.
PSA.126.6: Describing a farmer who sows in tears not knowing yet if the harvest will come, this psalm promises he will return with joyful shouts, carrying his sheaves.
PSA.130.5: Crying up from a place of deep distress, the psalmist describes waiting for the Lord the way someone might wait through a long night, hoping in his word.
PSA.138.3: David recalls a specific moment when he called out and God answered him, strengthening his soul at the very time he cried.
PSA.138.8: Trusting that God will finish what concerns him despite present trouble, David asks God not to abandon the work of his own hands.
PSA.145.9: In this alphabetic psalm of praise, David widens his focus from Israel alone to declare that the Lord's goodness and mercy extend over everything he made.
PSA.145.18: Still praising God's character in this acrostic psalm, David notes that the Lord stays near to everyone who calls on him sincerely.
PSA.146.5: After warning against trusting powerful people who eventually die, this psalm calls truly happy the one whose hope rests instead in the God of Jacob.
PSA.147.5: Praising God for both cosmic power and personal care, such as knowing every star by name, this psalm marvels that his understanding has no limit.
PSA.147.11: This psalm of praise notes that what pleases the Lord is not raw strength, like a fast horse, but people who fear him and hope in his mercy.
PRO.2.6: Addressing a son seeking wisdom, Solomon names the Lord himself as the actual source from which wisdom and knowledge come.
PRO.3.3: Instructing a son in wise living, Solomon urges him to hold onto mercy and truth so closely they become like something written on his own heart.
PRO.3.9: Continuing fatherly instruction on wise living, Solomon calls for honoring the Lord with material wealth, giving the first portion of one's income to him.
PRO.3.24: Part of a longer promise that wisdom brings safety, Solomon pictures a person lying down at night without fear and sleeping soundly.
PRO.4.18: Contrasting two ways of living, Solomon describes the righteous person's path as a light that keeps growing brighter until full daylight.
PRO.8.17: Speaking here in the voice of personified Wisdom herself, this saying promises that those who love and diligently seek her will find her.
PRO.10.22: Among Solomon's contrasts between the righteous and the wicked, he credits the Lord's blessing with bringing wealth that carries no accompanying grief.
PRO.10.28: Contrasting the outcomes awaiting the righteous and the wicked, Solomon promises hope brings gladness while wicked expectation comes to nothing.
PRO.11.25: Praising generosity, Solomon observes that the person who gives freely ends up enriched, and the one who refreshes others is refreshed in turn.
PRO.12.18: Contrasting careless and wise speech, Solomon compares reckless words to a sword's cutting wound, while the wise person's words bring healing.
PRO.12.28: Ending a chapter about diligence and honesty, Solomon ties the path of righteousness directly to life, with no death found along that way.
PRO.14.26: Among sayings on wisdom and family, Solomon links reverence for the Lord to a strong sense of security that extends even to one's children.
PRO.14.30: Comparing inward states rather than outward circumstances, Solomon credits a peaceful heart with giving life to the body, while envy rots it from within.
PRO.15.13: Turning to matters of the heart, Solomon observes that a cheerful heart shows on the face, while sorrow of heart breaks the spirit.
PRO.15.15: Continuing on inner disposition, Solomon contrasts the afflicted person's constant hardship with the merry heart's ongoing feast.
PRO.16.20: Linking practical skill to spiritual trust, Solomon promises good outcomes to whoever handles matters wisely and happiness to the one who trusts the Lord.
PRO.17.9: On handling another's fault, Solomon praises the one who covers an offense out of love, over the one who gossips and divides close friends.
PRO.19.11: Praising self-control over quick offense, Solomon credits wisdom with delaying anger, treating overlooking an insult as honorable rather than weak.
PRO.20.22: Countering the urge toward personal revenge, Solomon instructs the wronged person to wait on the Lord for deliverance instead of repaying evil directly.
PRO.20.24: Reflecting on how little control people actually have, Solomon notes that a person's steps are directed by the Lord, beyond full human understanding.
PRO.21.31: Closing a chapter weighing human planning against God's sovereignty, Solomon notes a war-horse can be readied, but victory ultimately belongs to the Lord.
PRO.22.4: Pairing two qualities together, Solomon credits humility joined with reverence for the Lord as the source of riches, honor, and a full life.
PRO.23.18: Advising against envying the apparent success of sinners, the father in this instruction assures his son there is a future ahead and hope will not be cut off.
PRO.24.10: Speaking plainly about crisis, Solomon observes that a person's true strength, or the lack of it, shows most clearly on a hard day.
PRO.24.14: Comparing wisdom to honey a son is urged to taste, Solomon promises that finding it brings a real future reward rather than disappointment.
PRO.25.11: Praising skillful communication, Solomon compares a well-timed word to gold fruit set in silver, an image of value matched to the right moment.
PRO.29.25: Contrasting two sources of security, Solomon warns that fearing what people think becomes a trap, while trusting the Lord keeps a person safe.
PRO.30.5: In sayings attributed to a lesser-known figure named Agur, this line affirms that every word from God is trustworthy, a shield for those who rely on him.
PRO.31.9: Part of a mother's instruction to her son, a king, this proverb charges him to speak up and judge fairly on behalf of the poor and needy.
PRO.31.10: Opening the closing poem of Proverbs, this verse poses a question about the rare value of a capable, virtuous woman, worth more than costly jewels.
ECC.2.24: After surveying all his labor and pleasure-seeking as ultimately empty, the Preacher concludes that simply enjoying food, drink, and work is itself a gift from God.
ECC.4.10: Reflecting on the value of companionship over isolation, the Preacher observes that a person who falls alone has no one there to help them up.
ECC.4.12: Continuing his praise of partnership over solitude, the Preacher notes that two can resist an attacker better than one, and three together are stronger still.
ECC.5.19: Commenting on wealth and enjoyment, the Preacher describes the ability to enjoy one's possessions and labor as itself a gift given by God, not something owed.
ECC.7.14: Weighing good days against bad ones, the Preacher advises enjoying prosperity while it lasts and reflecting during adversity, since God allows both to come.
ECC.11.5: Comparing the mystery of the wind and of a child forming in the womb, the Preacher argues that God's ways are simply beyond full human understanding.
SNG.2.16: In this love poem, the young woman describes her beloved as belonging entirely to her, picturing him among the lilies of the field.
SNG.4.7: Praising his bride in this love poem, the groom declares that she is completely beautiful to him, without a single flaw.
ISA.1.19: Calling Judah to account for its sin, God offers a choice through Isaiah: willing obedience will bring enjoyment of the land's good things, while rebellion brings the sword.
ISA.6.3: In Isaiah's vision of God's throne room, winged seraphim call to one another, declaring the Lord's holiness and the earth's fullness with his glory.
ISA.9.2: Describing relief for a people once oppressed in Galilee, Isaiah pictures a great light dawning on those who had been walking in darkness.
ISA.25.1: Opening a song of praise for God's deliverance, Isaiah exalts the Lord's name and credits him with faithfully carrying out ancient plans.
ISA.25.9: Looking ahead to a day when death itself is swallowed up, Isaiah pictures God's people finally saying that the Lord they waited for has brought salvation.
ISA.26.4: In a song anticipating Judah's future security, Isaiah urges trust in the Lord, describing him as an everlasting strength that never fails.
ISA.30.18: Even after describing Judah's stubborn refusal to trust him, God through Isaiah is shown waiting to be gracious, ready to show mercy to those who wait for him.
ISA.32.2: Describing the coming reign of a righteous king, Isaiah compares such leadership to shelter from wind and shade from a great rock in a dry land.
ISA.32.18: Looking past coming judgment to eventual restoration, Isaiah promises that God's people will finally dwell in peaceful, secure homes.
ISA.33.2: Facing an oppressive invader, Isaiah voices a prayer asking God to be gracious to a people who have been waiting for him and to be their strength each morning.
ISA.35.4: Speaking to those weakened by fear, Isaiah urges courage, promising that God himself is coming to bring vengeance on their behalf and save them.
ISA.40.1: Opening a new section of comfort after chapters of judgment, God instructs Isaiah to speak tenderly and repeatedly to his suffering people.
ISA.41.13: Reassuring an anxious Israel, God through Isaiah promises to hold their right hand personally and tells them plainly not to be afraid.
ISA.41.17: Picturing the desperate thirst of the poor, Isaiah has God promise that when they cry out for water, he himself, Israel's God, will answer and not abandon them.
ISA.42.16: Describing a coming deliverance for the blind and lost, God promises through Isaiah to guide them on unfamiliar paths and turn darkness into light before them.
ISA.44.22: Addressing Israel as his servant, God through Isaiah pictures their sins as a thick cloud he has already wiped away, and calls them back to himself.
ISA.46.4: Contrasting himself with idols that must be carried by their worshippers, God tells Israel through Isaiah that he is the one who carries his people, even into old age.
ISA.48.17: Identifying himself as Israel's Redeemer, God speaks through Isaiah as the teacher who instructs his people and leads them in the way they should go.
ISA.49.13: Announcing coming comfort for a people who felt abandoned, Isaiah calls the heavens and earth themselves to celebrate God's mercy toward the afflicted.
ISA.50.7: In this passage describing a suffering servant who endures shame without resisting, the speaker declares confidence that the Lord God will help and vindicate him.
ISA.54.10: Comparing God's covenant faithfulness to something more permanent than mountains, Isaiah promises that God's kindness toward his people will never depart.
ISA.55.6: Urging a response to God's offer of mercy, Isaiah calls people to seek the Lord while he can still be found and to call on him while he is near.
ISA.55.11: Comparing God's word to rain that reliably waters the earth and produces growth, Isaiah promises it will always accomplish what God intends and never return empty.
ISA.57.15: Describing God as both transcendent and near, Isaiah says the eternal, holy God chooses to dwell with those who are humble and repentant in heart.
ISA.58.11: Explaining what true fasting looks like, Isaiah promises that caring for the hungry and afflicted will bring the Lord's continual guidance and refreshment.
ISA.60.20: Picturing Jerusalem's future glory, Isaiah promises a light that never sets and an end to the mourning that once marked her days.
ISA.61.1: Speaking in the voice of an anointed messenger, Isaiah describes a mission to bring good news to the poor and freedom to captives, later read aloud by Jesus in Luke's Gospel.
ISA.63.9: Recalling Israel's history in the wilderness, Isaiah describes God as sharing personally in his people's suffering rather than watching from a distance.
ISA.65.17: Looking far beyond present judgment, God announces through Isaiah a coming new creation so complete that the old troubles will not even be remembered.
ISA.66.2: Even after describing the whole earth as his own creation, God says through Isaiah that he pays special attention to the humble person who trembles at his word.
JER.1.8: Called as a young prophet who protests he is too inexperienced to speak, Jeremiah is told by God not to fear, since God himself will be with him.
JER.3.22: Comparing Israel's unfaithfulness to a wandering spouse, God through Jeremiah still invites his rebellious people to return so he can heal what is broken.
JER.9.24: Contrasting worldly sources of pride, God tells Jeremiah that the only fitting boast is knowing God himself, the one who acts in kindness, justice, and righteousness.
JER.10.23: Reflecting on human limits, Jeremiah admits in prayer that people do not control the direction of their own lives, however carefully they plan.
JER.15.16: Despite his hard calling, Jeremiah tells God that receiving God's words brought him real joy, since he was known as one who carried God's name.
JER.17.14: Amid mockery for prophesying disaster that hasn't yet come, Jeremiah prays for personal healing, calling God his praise.
JER.20.11: Even while lamenting the mockery and plots against him, Jeremiah declares confidence that the Lord stands with him like a fearsome warrior, so his enemies will fail.
JER.31.13: Promising restoration after exile, God through Jeremiah pictures young and old dancing together as mourning turns into celebration.
JER.31.16: Continuing his promise of return from exile, God tells the grieving (pictured as Rachel weeping for her children) to stop weeping, since the exiled will come back.
JER.31.34: Describing a coming new covenant, God through Jeremiah promises to forgive Israel's sin completely and to be known personally by everyone, not taught secondhand.
JER.32.17: After buying a field as a sign of future hope even while Jerusalem is besieged, Jeremiah prays, marveling that nothing is too difficult for the God who made heaven and earth.
LAM.5.19: Closing this lament over Jerusalem's destruction, the poet turns from present ruin to the one unshaken fact: the Lord's own throne endures forever.
EZK.18.32: Rejecting the idea that he delights in judgment, God tells the exiled house of Israel through Ezekiel that he takes no pleasure in anyone's death and calls them to turn and live.
DAN.3.17: Facing execution in a furnace for refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego declare their confidence that God can deliver them.
DAN.3.18: Immediately after affirming God's power to save them, the three men add that even if he chooses not to, they will still refuse to worship the king's image.
DAN.6.10: Even after King Darius signs a decree banning prayer to anyone but himself, Daniel keeps his usual habit of praying toward Jerusalem three times a day.
HOS.2.19: Using marriage imagery for God's relationship with unfaithful Israel, Hosea has God promise a renewed covenant built on righteousness and lasting love.
HOS.6.1: Speaking as if voicing Israel's overdue repentance, Hosea urges the people to return to the Lord, trusting that the one who wounded them will also heal them.
HOS.6.3: Continuing that call to repentance, Hosea promises that pursuing knowledge of the Lord will bring him to his people as reliably as the seasonal rains.
HOS.10.12: Using farming imagery, Hosea urges Israel to plant righteousness and break up hardened ground, since it is time to seek the Lord.
HOS.11.4: Picturing God as a parent teaching a child to walk, Hosea describes God drawing wayward Israel gently, with cords of love rather than force.
JOL.2.13: Calling for genuine repentance rather than empty ritual, Joel urges the people to tear their hearts, not just their garments, trusting in God's mercy and slowness to anger.
AMO.3.7: Defending the legitimacy of prophetic warning, Amos states that the Lord acts only after revealing his plans in advance to his prophets.
OBA.1.17: After pronouncing judgment on Edom for its cruelty to Judah, Obadiah promises that deliverance and holiness will instead belong to Mount Zion.
JON.2.7: Praying from what he describes as the belly of the fish, Jonah recalls that even as his life was fainting, he remembered the Lord and his prayer reached God's temple.
MIC.7.7: Even as he laments betrayal within his own household and nation, Micah declares that he will keep looking to the Lord, confident God will hear him.
MIC.7.8: Addressing an enemy who expects to see him defeated, Micah answers that though he has fallen, he will rise, with the Lord himself as his light.
MIC.7.18: Closing his prophecy with praise rather than accusation, Micah marvels that God is unlike any other in his willingness to forgive and delight in mercy.
HAB.3.18: Even after describing crops failing and flocks disappearing, Habakkuk resolves to rejoice in the Lord regardless, since his joy rests in God as his salvation.
ZEP.3.14: Announcing coming restoration after judgment, Zephaniah calls Jerusalem, pictured as a daughter, to sing and rejoice with her whole heart.
HAG.2.9: Encouraging a discouraged people rebuilding a temple that seems less impressive than Solomon's, God promises through Haggai that its future glory will exceed the old.
ZEC.1.3: Opening his message to a people just returned from exile, Zechariah delivers God's invitation: turn back to me, and I will turn back to you.
ZEC.9.9: Announcing a coming king, Zechariah describes him as righteous and victorious yet arriving humbly on a donkey rather than a warhorse, a scene later echoed at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.
MAL.3.6: Reassuring a people who might doubt God's promises still apply, Malachi grounds their security in God's own unchanging character.
MAL.3.10: Challenging a people who had shortchanged their offerings, Malachi delivers God's invitation to test his generosity by bringing full tithes into the temple storehouse.
HEB.13.14: Urging readers to bear Christ's reproach rather than cling to earthly comforts, the writer explains that believers have no lasting city here, but are looking ahead to one still to come.
MAT.5.12: Closing the Beatitudes, Jesus tells his disciples that being insulted and persecuted for his sake places them in the same company as the prophets before them.
MAT.5.13: Right after the Beatitudes, Jesus tells his listeners they are salt to the earth, warning that salt which loses its flavor becomes useless.
MAT.6.8: Teaching about prayer in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his disciples not to babble on like others, since their Father already knows their needs before they ask.
MAT.6.20: Contrasting earthly and heavenly investment, Jesus urges his listeners to store up treasure in heaven, where nothing can decay or be stolen.
MAT.9.29: After two blind men ask Jesus for mercy and affirm their faith that he can heal them, he touches their eyes and restores their sight.
MAT.9.36: Seeing crowds who seem exhausted and directionless, Jesus responds not with frustration but with compassion, comparing them to sheep without a shepherd.
MAT.10.32: Sending out his twelve disciples, Jesus tells them that whoever publicly acknowledges him before others will be acknowledged by him before his Father.
MAT.11.6: Answering John the Baptist's disciples, who came asking whether Jesus is truly the promised one, Jesus pronounces a blessing on those who are not offended by him.
MAT.12.20: Quoting a prophecy from Isaiah about God's chosen servant, Matthew describes Jesus as one who deals gently with the weak rather than crushing them.
MAT.14.27: When the disciples see Jesus walking toward their boat on the water at night and cry out in fear, he immediately calls out to reassure them it is only him.
MAT.16.26: Teaching about the cost of following him, Jesus asks what value gaining the entire world would have if a person loses their own soul in the process.
MAT.17.7: After Peter, James, and John fall on their faces in fear at the transfiguration and the voice from the cloud, Jesus comes and tells them not to be afraid.
MAT.20.28: Correcting his disciples' ambitions for greatness, Jesus describes his own mission as coming to serve others and give his life for many.
MAT.23.11: Criticizing the status-seeking of the religious leaders, Jesus tells his followers that true greatness among them means becoming a servant.
MAT.24.13: Warning of coming persecution and deception before the end, Jesus promises that whoever endures faithfully to the end will be saved.
MAT.24.35: Speaking about the timing of future events only his Father knows, Jesus contrasts the eventual passing of heaven and earth with the permanence of his own words.
MAT.25.21: In the parable of the talents, a master praises the servant who invested his money well, welcoming him to share in his master's joy.
MRK.2.17: Confronted for eating with tax collectors and sinners, Jesus explains that he came specifically for people who know they need him, not those who think they don't.
LUK.1.45: Visited by her pregnant relative Mary, Elizabeth greets her with a blessing, praising her for believing what the Lord had promised her.
LUK.7.13: Encountering a widow burying her only son outside the town of Nain, Jesus is moved with compassion for her before he raises the young man back to life.
LUK.8.15: Explaining the parable of the sower, Jesus describes the good soil as people who hear God's word with an honest heart and patiently produce fruit.
LUK.10.42: Visiting the home of Martha and Mary, Jesus gently tells the busy, distracted Martha that Mary, who sat listening to him, had chosen the one thing that truly matters.
LUK.11.28: After a woman praises the mother who bore him, Jesus redirects the blessing toward anyone who hears and keeps God's word.
LUK.12.40: Teaching his disciples to stay alert, Jesus compares his own unexpected return to a thief arriving at an hour no one anticipates.
LUK.14.11: At a dinner where guests jockey for the best seats, Jesus teaches that whoever exalts himself will be humbled, while the humble will be honored.
LUK.16.13: Concluding a parable about a dishonest steward, Jesus warns that no one can fully serve both God and money at the same time.
LUK.17.21: Answering Pharisees who ask when God's kingdom will arrive, Jesus tells them it will not come as a visible spectacle, since it is already present among them.
LUK.18.1: Introducing a parable about a persistent widow and an unjust judge, Luke notes that Jesus told it to teach his disciples to keep praying and never give up.
LUK.21.28: Describing frightening signs before his return, Jesus tells his disciples that when these things begin, they should look up rather than despair, because rescue is near.
LUK.22.32: Warning Peter that Satan wants to test him, Jesus says he has already prayed for Peter's faith to hold, so that Peter can later strengthen the other disciples.
LUK.23.43: Responding to a criminal crucified beside him who asks to be remembered, Jesus promises that they will be together in paradise that very day.
LUK.24.32: After the risen but unrecognized Jesus explains the scriptures to two travelers on the road to Emmaus, they later recall how their hearts burned within them as he spoke.
JHN.1.4: Opening his Gospel with cosmic language about the eternal Word, John states that life itself was found in him, a life that became light for humanity.
JHN.1.16: Reflecting on Jesus as the Word made flesh, John describes believers as continually receiving grace upon grace out of his abundant fullness.
JHN.1.29: Seeing Jesus approach him at the Jordan, John the Baptist points him out to the crowd, naming him the Lamb of God who takes away the world's sin.
JHN.3.3: Answering Nicodemus, a Pharisee who comes to him at night, Jesus insists that seeing God's kingdom requires nothing less than being born again.
JHN.4.14: Talking with a Samaritan woman at a well, Jesus contrasts ordinary water with the water he offers, which permanently satisfies and leads to eternal life.
JHN.5.24: Speaking about the authority given to him by the Father, Jesus promises that whoever hears his word and believes has already crossed from death into life.
JHN.7.38: Standing up during the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus cries out that whoever believes in him will have rivers of living water flowing from within them.
JHN.8.11: Facing a woman brought to him after being caught in adultery, Jesus declines to condemn her, telling her instead to go and leave her sin behind.
JHN.8.36: Speaking to Jews who claim never to have been enslaved, Jesus tells them that real freedom, the kind he offers, is the only freedom that lasts.
JHN.9.3: When his disciples ask whose sin caused a man's blindness from birth, Jesus rejects that framing, saying instead that God's work would be displayed through him.
JHN.10.28: Describing himself as the good shepherd, Jesus promises his sheep eternal life so secure that no one can snatch them out of his hand.
JHN.11.40: Just before raising Lazarus from the dead, Jesus reminds Martha of what he had already told her: that believing would let her see God's glory.
JHN.14.13: Promising his disciples continued access to the Father after his departure, Jesus assures them that whatever they ask in his name he will do.
JHN.14.21: In his farewell teaching before the crucifixion, Jesus links obedience to his commandments with love, promising to reveal himself to those who love him that way.
JHN.15.4: Using the image of a vine and its branches, Jesus tells his disciples that fruitfulness depends entirely on staying connected to him.
JHN.15.9: Continuing the vine imagery, Jesus tells his disciples that just as the Father has loved him, he has loved them, and calls them to remain in that love.
JHN.15.11: Explaining why he has shared this teaching about abiding in his love, Jesus says it is so that his own joy might fill his disciples completely.
JHN.16.24: Preparing his disciples for prayer after his departure, Jesus tells them that asking in his name, something they had not yet done, will bring them full joy.
JHN.17.3: Praying aloud before his arrest, Jesus defines eternal life not as an abstract reward but as truly knowing the Father and Jesus Christ, whom he sent.
JHN.20.19: On the evening of his resurrection, Jesus appears to his frightened disciples behind locked doors and greets them simply with peace.
ACT.2.42: Describing the earliest church in Jerusalem after Pentecost, Luke notes their steady devotion to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, shared meals, and prayer.
ACT.3.19: Preaching to the crowd after healing a lame man, Peter calls them to repent and turn back to God so their sins can be wiped away.
ACT.4.20: Ordered by the Jewish authorities to stop preaching about Jesus, Peter and John reply simply that they cannot help speaking about what they have seen and heard.
ACT.4.32: Describing the unity of the early Jerusalem believers, Luke notes that they shared everything freely, with no one treating their possessions as strictly their own.
ACT.9.6: Struck blind and thrown to the ground on the road to Damascus, Saul asks the voice of the risen Jesus what he should do, and is told to go into the city for instructions.
ACT.10.43: Preaching to the Roman centurion Cornelius and his household, Peter declares that all the prophets testified that faith in Jesus brings forgiveness of sins.
ACT.13.39: Preaching in a synagogue in Antioch, Paul tells his Jewish listeners that faith in Jesus brings a justification the law of Moses could never provide.
ACT.14.17: Speaking to a crowd in Lystra who want to worship him and Barnabas as gods, Paul insists God has always shown himself through good gifts like rain and harvest.
ACT.15.11: At the council in Jerusalem debating whether Gentile believers must follow the law of Moses, Peter argues that salvation comes through grace, the same way for everyone.
ACT.20.24: Bidding farewell to the Ephesian elders before a dangerous journey to Jerusalem, Paul says he does not treasure his own life above finishing the ministry he was given.
ACT.27.25: During a violent storm at sea threatening the ship carrying him to Rome, Paul encourages the crew, telling them to take heart because an angel promised their safety.
ROM.1.17: Introducing the theme of his letter to Rome, Paul explains that the gospel reveals a righteousness that comes by faith, quoting the prophet Habakkuk.
ROM.6.4: Explaining what baptism symbolizes, Paul describes believers as buried with Christ so that they can walk in a genuinely new kind of life, just as he was raised.
ROM.7.24: Wrestling with the ongoing struggle between wanting to do good and actually doing it, Paul cries out in frustration, asking who can rescue him from this conflict.
ROM.8.14: Contrasting a life driven by the flesh with one guided by God's Spirit, Paul identifies those led by the Spirit as God's own children.
ROM.8.32: Building toward his argument that nothing can separate believers from God's love, Paul reasons that a God who already gave up his own Son will certainly not withhold anything else good.
ROM.9.16: Discussing God's sovereign choice in showing mercy to Moses and Pharaoh, Paul concludes that mercy depends on God's will, not on human effort or desire.
ROM.10.17: Explaining how people come to believe, Paul traces faith back to hearing, and hearing back to the message about Christ being preached.
ROM.11.36: Closing a long discussion of Israel's place in God's plan, Paul breaks into praise, declaring that everything comes from, through, and returns to God.
ROM.12.9: Moving from doctrine to practical instruction, Paul urges the Roman believers toward sincere love, rejecting evil and holding fast to what is good.
ROM.13.8: In a section on civil obligations and neighborly duty, Paul reduces every debt to one that never fully closes: the ongoing obligation to love one another.
ROM.14.8: Addressing disputes among believers over disputable matters, Paul reminds them that whether living or dying, they belong entirely to the Lord.
ROM.14.17: Correcting a focus on food regulations that was dividing the Roman church, Paul insists God's kingdom is really about righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.
ROM.15.1: Addressing tension between believers with different convictions about disputed practices, Paul tells those with stronger faith to bear with the weak rather than please only themselves.
ROM.16.20: Near the close of his letter, Paul warns against those causing division and promises that God will soon crush Satan's influence underfoot.
1CO.1.9: Opening his letter to a divided Corinthian church, Paul grounds their calling not in their own consistency but in the faithfulness of the God who called them.
1CO.1.18: Addressing a church impressed by clever rhetoric, Paul insists that the message of the cross, though it looks foolish to some, carries the very power of God to those being saved.
1CO.3.11: Warning against building the church on human wisdom or personality, Paul insists that Jesus Christ alone is the only foundation that can ever be laid.
1CO.4.20: Responding to some in Corinth who talk boldly but live carelessly, Paul contrasts empty words with the real power that marks God's kingdom.
1CO.10.31: Concluding a section about food, conscience, and Christian liberty, Paul gives a broad principle: whatever believers do, even eating and drinking, should aim at God's glory.
1CO.11.1: Closing a section about giving up personal preference for others' benefit, Paul urges the Corinthians to imitate him, just as he imitates Christ.
1CO.12.4: Introducing his teaching on spiritual gifts, Paul notes that though believers' gifts vary widely, they all come from the same Spirit.
1CO.14.1: Shifting from his teaching on love in chapter 13 back to spiritual gifts, Paul urges the Corinthians to pursue love while still desiring gifts, especially prophecy.
1CO.15.20: Defending the reality of the resurrection against doubters in Corinth, Paul declares that Christ has already been raised, becoming the first of many who will follow.
2CO.2.14: Reflecting on the emotional toll of ministry and reunion with Titus, Paul thanks God for making him and his coworkers part of Christ's ongoing victory.
2CO.3.18: Contrasting the old covenant's veiled glory with life under the Spirit, Paul describes believers as gradually being transformed to reflect the Lord's own likeness.
2CO.4.8: Describing the hardships of his ministry, Paul lists paradoxes of trouble without despair and difficulty without abandonment.
2CO.4.17: Weighing present suffering against future glory, Paul calls his own hardships a light, momentary affliction compared to the eternal weight of glory ahead.
2CO.5.20: Explaining the message entrusted to believers, Paul describes himself and his coworkers as Christ's ambassadors, pleading with people to be reconciled to God.
2CO.6.2: Quoting the prophet Isaiah about a favorable moment of salvation, Paul urges the Corinthians to respond to God's grace now rather than let it pass unused.
2CO.7.10: Distinguishing two kinds of regret, Paul explains that sorrow leading to genuine repentance brings salvation, while worldly sorrow only leads to death.
2CO.8.9: Urging the Corinthians toward generosity, Paul points them to Christ's own example, who became poor for their sake so that they could become rich.
2CO.9.8: Encouraging cheerful giving toward a collection for needy believers, Paul assures the Corinthians that God is able to supply all their needs so they can keep giving.
2CO.12.10: Reflecting on a persistent affliction he calls a thorn in the flesh, Paul concludes he can actually take pleasure in weakness, since it is there Christ's power shows most.
2CO.13.11: Closing his second letter to a troubled church, Paul urges the Corinthians toward unity, comfort, and peace, promising that God will be with them.
GAL.3.26: Arguing that the law's role was temporary, Paul tells the Galatians that through faith in Christ Jesus they are now fully recognized as God's own children.
GAL.4.6: Describing the new relationship believers have with God, Paul says the Spirit of God's own Son now cries out from within them, addressing God as Father.
GAL.5.13: Warning against misusing Christian freedom, Paul tells the Galatians their liberty was never meant to serve selfish desire, but to serve one another in love.
GAL.5.16: Contrasting life directed by the Spirit with life driven by sinful desire, Paul instructs the Galatians to walk in the Spirit as the way to resist the flesh's pull.
GAL.5.25: Closing his list of the Spirit's fruit, Paul urges believers who already live by the Spirit to also let the Spirit direct how they walk day to day.
EPH.1.3: Opening this letter with praise, Paul blesses God for the spiritual blessings believers already have in Christ, before turning to explain what those blessings include.
EPH.4.29: Giving practical instruction on speech, Paul tells believers to avoid corrupting talk and instead speak in ways that build others up and minister grace.
EPH.5.1: Transitioning into ethical instruction, Paul calls believers to imitate God the way children naturally imitate a loving parent.
EPH.5.8: Reminding the Ephesians of who they now are, Paul contrasts their former life in spiritual darkness with their present identity as people who live in the light.
EPH.6.13: Describing the Christian life as a spiritual battle, Paul urges believers to put on God's full armor so they can stand firm when trouble comes.
PHP.4.9: Closing a series of practical exhortations, Paul tells the Philippians to actually practice what they learned from watching his own life, promising God's peace will follow.
COL.2.10: Countering teachings that add extra spiritual requirements, Paul insists believers already have everything they need through their union with Christ.
COL.3.1: Having described believers as raised with Christ through baptism, Paul urges them to set their minds on heavenly realities rather than earthly ones.
COL.3.14: After listing virtues like kindness and patience believers should put on, Paul names love as the one that binds all the others together into unity.
COL.3.23: Giving instructions to servants within Colossian households, Paul tells them to do their work wholeheartedly, as if serving the Lord rather than a human master.
1TH.4.18: Having just described believers being reunited with the Lord and with loved ones who have died, Paul tells the Thessalonians to use these words to comfort one another.
1TH.5.16: Among a rapid series of short instructions closing his letter, Paul tells the Thessalonians simply to rejoice continually.
1TH.5.24: Praying that God would keep the Thessalonians blameless until Christ's return, Paul grounds that hope not in their effort but in the faithfulness of the one who calls them.
2TH.3.13: Addressing believers frustrated by others who refuse to work, Paul still urges the whole church not to grow weary in doing what is right.
1TI.1.15: Recalling his own past as a persecutor of the church, Paul calls it a trustworthy saying that Christ came to save sinners, naming himself as the worst example of one.
1TI.1.17: After marveling at the mercy shown to him despite his past, Paul breaks into a short doxology praising the eternal, invisible, only God.
1TI.2.5: Arguing for prayer on behalf of all people, Paul grounds that universal appeal in the fact that there is only one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, for everyone.
1TI.6.12: Warning Timothy against the love of money, Paul instead urges him to pursue righteousness and fight faithfully for the eternal life he has already professed.
2TI.1.12: Even while suffering for the gospel, Paul tells Timothy he is not ashamed, because he is confident in the one he has trusted to guard what has been entrusted to him.
2TI.4.8: Nearing the end of his life, Paul describes a crown of righteousness waiting for him and for everyone who has longed for Christ's return.
2TI.4.17: Recalling a moment when everyone abandoned him at trial, Paul credits the Lord alone with standing by him and giving him strength to keep preaching.
TIT.3.5: Reminding Titus of the believers' own past folly, Paul insists that salvation came not through good deeds but through God's mercy and the Spirit's renewing work.
PHM.1.7: Writing to Philemon about his slave Onesimus, Paul first expresses genuine joy over reports of Philemon's love, which has refreshed other believers.
HEB.3.13: Warning against the danger of gradually hardening toward God, the writer urges believers to encourage each other daily while there is still time.
HEB.4.9: Comparing the promised land's rest to something still available under a new covenant, the writer declares that a Sabbath rest remains for God's people.
HEB.10.23: Encouraging believers to draw near to God with confidence, the writer urges them to hold firmly to their hope, trusting that God keeps his promises.
HEB.10.36: Encouraging believers who had already lost possessions for their faith, the writer tells them they need endurance so they can eventually receive what God promised.
HEB.11.3: Opening his survey of Old Testament examples of faith, the writer states that faith itself is what lets people understand that God's word brought the visible world into being.
HEB.11.13: Reflecting on figures like Abraham and Sarah who died without seeing God's promises fulfilled, the writer notes they still held onto faith, calling themselves strangers on earth.
HEB.12.1: Having just listed generations of faithful witnesses, the writer urges believers to strip away anything that weighs them down and run their own race with endurance.
HEB.12.6: Comparing God's discipline to a father's correction of a beloved child, the writer explains that God's chastening is actually proof of his love.
HEB.12.14: Urging practical holiness among believers, the writer calls them to pursue peace with everyone and the kind of holiness without which no one will see God.
HEB.13.1: Opening his closing exhortations, the writer simply instructs believers to keep on loving one another as they have been doing.
HEB.13.6: Quoting an Old Testament promise that God will never abandon his people, the writer encourages believers to speak boldly, unafraid of what anyone can do to them.
HEB.13.15: Describing worship appropriate for people without an earthly altar or lasting city, the writer calls believers to continually offer God praise through their words.
JAS.1.2: Writing to Jewish believers scattered by persecution, James startles them with an unexpected instruction: to consider it pure joy whenever they face various trials.
JAS.4.10: Calling for genuine repentance rather than surface-level religion, James tells his readers to humble themselves before the Lord, who will then lift them up.
JAS.5.11: Pointing to the patience of Job as an example worth remembering, James assures suffering believers that the Lord is compassionate and full of tender mercy.
1PE.1.8: Writing to believers scattered across Asia Minor who have never seen Jesus in person, Peter describes their love for him and their joy as real even without sight.
1PE.2.24: Describing Christ's suffering as an example for mistreated believers to follow, Peter says Christ bore their sins on the cross so they could live for righteousness instead.
1PE.3.4: Instructing wives about true beauty, Peter contrasts outward adornment with the inner qualities of a gentle and quiet spirit that God finds precious.
1PE.4.19: Addressing believers suffering for their faith, Peter tells them to entrust their souls to God, the faithful Creator, while continuing to do what is right.
2PE.1.10: Urging believers to actively grow in the qualities of faith he has just listed, Peter tells them that doing so will confirm their calling and keep them from falling.
2PE.3.8: Answering scoffers who doubt Christ's promised return because time has passed, Peter reminds believers that God does not measure time the way people do.
1JN.1.7: Contrasting life in the light with life in darkness, John tells believers that walking in God's light brings genuine fellowship and cleansing through Christ's blood.
1JN.2.25: Reassuring believers being pressured by false teachers, John reminds them that the promise Christ gave them, eternal life, still stands.
1JN.5.4: Explaining what genuine faith produces, John declares that everyone born of God has the power to overcome the world, through faith itself.
2JN.1.6: Writing to a Christian woman and her children, John ties love directly to obedience, defining love as simply walking according to God's commandments.
3JN.1.11: Contrasting a divisive church leader named Diotrephes with a well-regarded believer named Demetrius, John urges his reader, Gaius, to imitate what is good rather than evil.
JUD.1.2: Opening his short letter with a greeting rather than his planned topic, Jude prays that mercy, peace, and love would increase abundantly among his readers.
REV.1.18: Appearing to John in an overwhelming vision, the risen Christ identifies himself as the one who was dead but now lives forever, holding power over death itself.
REV.3.5: In a message to the church at Sardis, Christ promises that whoever remains faithful will be dressed in white and will have his name openly acknowledged before the Father.
REV.21.1: Describing a climactic vision, John sees an entirely new heaven and earth replace the old one, with even the sea no longer present.
REV.21.7: Speaking from his throne about the new creation, God promises that whoever perseveres will inherit everything and be called his own son.
REV.22.13: Near the very end of the book, Christ identifies himself using titles that span all of time, calling himself the Alpha and Omega, the first and the last.
REV.22.17: In the Bible's closing invitation, both the Spirit and the church call out for anyone who is thirsty to come and freely take the water of life.
GEN.21.17: Sent into the desert with her son and out of water, Hagar sits apart so she won't watch him die, until an angel calls to her.
GEN.22.14: After God stops him from sacrificing Isaac and provides a ram instead, Abraham names the mountain for what God did there.
GEN.32.26: Wrestling through the night with a mysterious man at a river crossing, Jacob refuses to let go even as dawn breaks.
GEN.33.4: Jacob returns home braced for revenge from the brother he cheated years earlier, but Esau runs to meet him and embraces him instead.
GEN.39.21: Falsely accused and thrown into an Egyptian prison, Joseph finds that God has not left him even there.
GEN.45.15: Having just revealed himself to the brothers who sold him into slavery, Joseph weeps over each of them and welcomes them back.
GEN.50.21: After their father dies, Joseph's brothers fear he will finally take revenge, but he reassures them and promises to care for their families.
GEN.2.7: In the second creation account, the narrator describes God shaping the first human from dust and breathing life into him.
EXO.23.20: As Israel prepares to leave Mount Sinai for an unknown land, God promises to send an angel ahead to guard them on the way.
EXO.33.19: When Moses asks to see God's glory, God answers by promising to show him his goodness and speak his own name.
EXO.14.13: Trapped between the sea and Pharaoh's approaching army, the terrified Israelites hear Moses tell them to stand still and watch God act.
LEV.19.32: Among laws about how to treat one another, God tells Israel to stand up for the elderly and show them honor.
DEU.4.31: Moses warns Israel they may one day drift from God, then assures them that if they turn back, God will not abandon them.
DEU.8.3: Looking back on forty years in the wilderness, Moses explains why God let the people go hungry and then fed them with manna.
DEU.31.8: Moses, about to die and hand leadership to Joshua, tells him in front of all Israel that God will go ahead of him.
DEU.33.12: In his final blessing over the tribes of Israel, Moses describes the tribe of Benjamin resting safely in God's care.
DEU.33.25: Blessing the tribe of Asher at the end of his life, Moses prays that their strength would last as long as their days.
JOS.1.5: Speaking to Joshua right after Moses' death, God promises to be with him in the same way he was with Moses.
JOS.23.14: Old and near death, Joshua gathers Israel's leaders and reminds them that every one of God's promises to them came true.
JDG.6.23: After realizing he has been speaking with the angel of the LORD, Gideon fears for his life, and God tells him he will not die.
JDG.6.24: Relieved after his encounter with the angel, Gideon builds an altar and gives it a name that means 'the LORD is peace.'
RUT.4.14: After Naomi lost her husband and both sons, the women of Bethlehem celebrate with her when her family line is restored through Ruth.
1SA.2.8: Hannah, who had long been mocked for being childless, sings this prayer after God answers her request for a son.
1SA.17.47: Facing the giant Goliath with only a sling, the young shepherd David declares that the battle belongs to God, not to weapons.
1SA.12.22: Samuel, stepping back from leading Israel, assures the people that God will not abandon them despite their mistakes.
2SA.7.18: After God promises that David's family will rule forever, David sits before God and asks, amazed, why he has been treated so well.
2SA.9.7: Now king, David seeks out Mephibosheth, the disabled grandson of his old rival Saul, to show him kindness for Jonathan's sake.
2SA.12.23: After his infant son dies, David stops fasting and explains to his confused servants how he has come to terms with the loss.
2SA.18.33: David hears that his son Absalom, who led a rebellion against him, has been killed, and he breaks down in grief.
1KI.8.56: At the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem, King Solomon blesses God for keeping every promise he made through Moses.
1KI.19.7: Exhausted and wanting to die after fleeing for his life, the prophet Elijah is woken a second time by an angel with food.
1CH.16.8: After the ark of God is brought into Jerusalem, David gives the temple singers this song of thanks to perform.
1CH.29.14: As the people give generously to build the temple, David prays in wonder that everything they are giving came from God first.
2CH.20.12: Facing an invading army far larger than his own, King Jehoshaphat stands before the people and admits to God that they don't know what to do.
2CH.32.7: As the Assyrian army surrounds Jerusalem, King Hezekiah gathers his military officers and tells them not to be afraid.
EZR.3.11: When the exiles returning from Babylon lay the foundation of a new temple, the people break out in songs of thanks.
NEH.9.17: In a long prayer confessing Israel's history of rebellion, the Levites recall that God kept forgiving them anyway.
JOB.5.18: Job's friend Eliphaz, trying to comfort him in his suffering, describes God as one who wounds but also heals.
JOB.8.21: Bildad, another of Job's friends, tells Job that God will one day fill his mouth with laughter again.
JOB.12.10: Responding to his friends, Job says that every creature's life, and every human breath, rests in God's hand.
JOB.36.15: Elihu, a younger man who speaks after Job's friends, argues that God uses suffering to open people's ears.
JOB.14.7: Reflecting on how short human life is, Job notes with longing that even a tree that has been cut down can grow back.
PSA.3.5: David writes this psalm while fleeing from his son Absalom, marveling that he could still sleep and wake up safe.
PSA.4.7: In an evening prayer, David says the joy God has given him is greater than the joy of a rich harvest.
PSA.5.11: In a morning prayer for protection, David asks God to let everyone who takes refuge in him sing for joy.
PSA.5.12: Closing a morning prayer, David pictures God's favor surrounding the righteous like a soldier's shield.
PSA.6.2: Sick and in anguish, David begs God to be gentle with him and heal him.
PSA.6.6: In one of the Bible's most raw prayers of sorrow, David describes crying so much at night that his bed is soaked.
PSA.6.9: After pouring out his grief, David suddenly speaks with confidence that God has heard him.
PSA.8.5: Looking at the night sky and wondering why God cares about humans at all, David marvels at the honor God has given them.
PSA.9.1: David opens this psalm by promising to thank God wholeheartedly and to tell others about everything God has done.
PSA.9.18: In a psalm about God's justice, David insists that poor and forgotten people will not stay forgotten forever.
PSA.10.14: After describing how the wicked prey on the helpless, the psalm's writer says God sees it all and helps those with no one else.
PSA.12.6: Surrounded by people who flatter and lie, David contrasts their words with God's, which he says are pure like refined silver.
PSA.13.1: David opens this short psalm with an honest cry, asking God how long he will feel forgotten and alone.
PSA.16.2: David writes this psalm about finding safety in God, saying nothing good in his life exists apart from him.
PSA.16.5: David describes God as his portion and his cup, the share of life he has been given and is content with.
PSA.16.6: Using the picture of land being divided up by boundary lines, David says the life God has given him is a good one.
PSA.17.8: Surrounded by enemies, David asks God to guard him as closely as a person guards the pupil of their own eye.
PSA.18.6: Written after God rescued him from Saul, this psalm has David remembering how he cried out when he was in danger.
PSA.18.16: Describing his rescue in vivid poetic terms, David pictures God reaching down and pulling him out of deep water.
PSA.18.19: Celebrating his rescue from his enemies, David says God saved him simply because God delighted in him.
PSA.18.28: In his song of thanks for being rescued, David says it is God who lights his lamp when everything around him is dark.
PSA.18.30: Looking back on how God protected him, David says God's way is perfect and his word can be trusted completely.
PSA.18.35: Thanking God for victory, David says it was God's gentleness, not his own strength, that lifted him up.
PSA.19.8: After praising God's glory in the sky, David turns to praise God's instructions, which he says bring joy to the heart.
PSA.19.10: Still reflecting on God's instructions, David says they are worth more than gold and sweeter than honey.
PSA.19.12: After praising God's law, David admits he can't see all of his own faults and asks God to cleanse the hidden ones.
PSA.22.4: In the middle of a psalm that begins 'why have you forsaken me,' David remembers that his ancestors trusted God and were rescued.
PSA.22.5: Still feeling abandoned, David recalls that those before him cried out to God and were never let down.
PSA.22.11: Surrounded by enemies and feeling alone, David asks God not to stay far away when trouble is so close.
PSA.22.19: Near the turning point of his lament, David calls God his strength and begs him to come quickly.
PSA.25.5: In a prayer written as a Hebrew acrostic, David asks God to guide him and teach him the right way to live.
PSA.25.6: Asking for forgiveness, David appeals to God to remember his own long history of compassion and mercy.
PSA.25.9: David says that God leads and teaches people who are humble enough to be taught.
PSA.25.10: Continuing his prayer for guidance, David says every path God leads people on is marked by love and faithfulness.
PSA.25.11: David openly admits his wrongdoing is great and asks God to forgive it for the sake of his own name.
PSA.25.16: Near the end of this prayer, David asks God to turn toward him, because he feels lonely and troubled.
PSA.25.17: David describes the troubles of his heart growing larger and asks God to bring him out of his distress.
PSA.25.18: David asks God to look at his suffering and, at the same time, to take away all of his sins.
PSA.26.2: Accused of wrongdoing, David asks God himself to examine his heart and mind and judge him honestly.
PSA.27.4: In a psalm about trusting God when enemies surround him, David says the one thing he wants most is to be near God.
PSA.27.5: David says that when trouble comes, God will hide him away in his shelter and set him high on a rock.
PSA.27.8: David describes his own heart urging him to seek God's face, and says he will.
PSA.28.8: Having cried out for help at the start of this psalm, David ends by calling God the strength of all his people.
PSA.30.2: David writes this psalm after recovering from a life-threatening illness, remembering that God healed him when he cried for help.
PSA.31.3: Hunted by enemies, David asks God to be his rock and fortress and to lead him for the sake of his name.
PSA.31.5: David entrusts his life into God's hands, words Jesus would later pray from the cross.
PSA.31.7: David says he will rejoice in God's love, because God has seen his suffering and knows how deeply he is hurting.
PSA.31.9: David describes being worn down by grief so heavy that it affects his eyes, his soul and his body.
PSA.31.14: Right after describing how his friends and neighbors have turned against him, David declares that he will still trust God.
PSA.31.19: David stops to marvel at how much goodness God has stored up for the people who take refuge in him.
PSA.32.5: David describes how he finally stopped hiding his wrongdoing and confessed it, and how God forgave him.
PSA.32.10: After describing the relief of being forgiven, David says God's love surrounds everyone who trusts him.
PSA.33.4: In a psalm of praise, the writer says God's word is right and everything God does can be trusted.
PSA.33.22: The psalm's writer closes with a simple prayer that God's love would rest on the people who hope in him.
PSA.34.1: Written after David escaped danger by pretending to be insane before a foreign king, this psalm opens with a promise to always praise God.
PSA.34.5: David says people who look to God are radiant with joy and will never need to hide their faces in shame.
PSA.34.10: David contrasts hungry young lions with those who seek God, who he says will not lack any good thing.
PSA.34.22: David ends this psalm by saying God rescues his servants and no one who takes refuge in him will be condemned.
PSA.36.9: Having just described the wickedness of the human heart, David turns to God as the source of life and light.
PSA.37.24: In a psalm urging patience while wrongdoers seem to prosper, David says a good person may stumble but God holds their hand.
PSA.37.25: Now old, David says that in all his years he has never seen those who trust God abandoned.
PSA.37.37: David tells his readers to pay attention to people of integrity, because a future awaits those who pursue peace.
PSA.37.39: David closes this long psalm by saying that God is the stronghold of those who do right when trouble comes.
PSA.38.9: Sick, in pain and ashamed of his wrongdoing, David tells God that every longing and groan he has is already known to him.
PSA.38.15: Surrounded by people who want him to fail, David says he will wait for God, confident that God will answer.
PSA.38.21: David ends this painful prayer by asking God not to abandon him or stay far away.
PSA.39.4: Troubled by how short life is, David asks God to help him understand how few his days really are.
PSA.39.12: David asks God to hear his tears, describing himself as a traveler just passing through this life, like his ancestors.
PSA.40.3: After God lifted him out of a pit, David says he was given a new song to sing that would lead others to trust God.
PSA.40.5: David says God's wonders and plans for his people are too many to count or describe.
PSA.40.17: Ending this psalm in need, David calls himself poor and needy and asks God to think of him and not delay.
PSA.42.8: Feeling far from God and discouraged, the psalm's writer remembers that God's love is present by day and his song by night.
PSA.43.3: Continuing the lament of the psalm before it, the writer asks God to send his light and truth to lead him home.
PSA.43.4: Still far from the temple, the writer imagines returning to the altar of God and calls God his greatest joy.
PSA.46.7: In a psalm about staying unafraid even if the earth gives way, this refrain repeats that the LORD of hosts is with his people as their fortress.
PSA.48.14: After touring Jerusalem's walls in celebration, the psalm's writers say God will guide his people until the very end.
PSA.49.15: Reflecting on how death comes for rich and poor alike, the psalm's writer says God will rescue his life from the grave.
PSA.51.1: Written after the prophet Nathan confronted him over his adultery with Bathsheba, David opens by begging God for mercy.
PSA.51.2: In his prayer of confession after his affair with Bathsheba, David asks God to wash him completely clean.
PSA.51.7: David asks God to make him clean again, using an image of being washed whiter than snow.
PSA.51.17: David says that what God truly wants is not animal sacrifices but a humble, broken heart.
PSA.52.8: Contrasting himself with a powerful man who trusted in his wealth, David pictures himself as an olive tree flourishing in God's house.
PSA.55.16: Betrayed by a close friend, David says he will call on God, confident that God will save him.
PSA.56.9: Hunted by enemies, David says that whenever he cries out, he knows God is on his side.
PSA.57.2: Hiding from King Saul in a cave, David cries out to God, who he says will fulfill his purpose for him.
PSA.57.10: Still in the cave, David praises God's love as reaching higher than the heavens.
PSA.59.16: While Saul's men watch his house to kill him, David says he will sing each morning about God's strength and love.
PSA.61.3: Praying from what feels like the ends of the earth, David remembers that God has always been his refuge and strong tower.
PSA.61.4: Far from home, David asks to live in God's presence forever, sheltered under his wings like a young bird.

JHN.21.17: Jesus asks Peter a third time if he loves him, and Peter, hurt, answers that Jesus knows everything.
ACT.2.28: Preaching on the day of Pentecost, Peter quotes a psalm of David about the joy of being in God's presence.
ACT.5.41: After being flogged and ordered to stop speaking about Jesus, the apostles leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy.
ACT.7.60: As he is being stoned to death for his faith, Stephen kneels and asks God not to hold it against his killers.
ACT.13.38: Preaching in a synagogue in Antioch of Pisidia, Paul announces that forgiveness of sins is offered through Jesus.
ACT.18.9: While facing opposition in Corinth, Paul has a vision at night in which the Lord tells him not to be afraid.
ACT.18.10: Continuing Paul's night vision in Corinth, the Lord promises to be with him and says many people in the city belong to him.
ACT.27.22: Caught in a violent storm at sea for days, Paul stands up among the terrified sailors and urges them to take courage.
ROM.5.6: Writing to the church in Rome, Paul explains that Christ died for people at the very moment they were powerless to help themselves.
ROM.5.10: Paul reasons that if God made peace with people while they were still his enemies, he will surely keep saving them now.
ROM.8.15: Paul tells the Roman believers they have not been given a spirit that makes them afraid, but one that lets them call God 'Father.'
ROM.8.17: Paul explains that as God's children, believers are also heirs who will share in Christ's glory after sharing in his suffering.
ROM.8.34: Near the climax of his letter's most hopeful chapter, Paul asks who could possibly condemn those Christ himself is praying for.
ROM.12.10: In a list of practical instructions for Christian community, Paul urges the Romans to love each other like family.
ROM.12.12: Paul gives the Roman church a short three-part instruction for enduring hard times.
ROM.12.13: Continuing his practical instructions, Paul urges believers to share with those in need and welcome strangers into their homes.
ROM.12.16: Paul encourages the Roman church to live in harmony and to be willing to spend time with people of low position.
ROM.12.17: Teaching how to respond to mistreatment, Paul tells the Romans not to pay anyone back with evil.
ROM.12.19: Paul tells believers not to take revenge themselves, but to leave judgment in God's hands.
ROM.14.19: In a section about believers who disagree over food and holy days, Paul urges them to pursue peace and build one another up.
1CO.1.27: Writing to a church proud of its status and cleverness, Paul points out that God deliberately chose people the world considered weak.
1CO.6.20: Paul reminds the Corinthian believers that they were bought at a price, so their bodies belong to God.
1CO.15.54: In his long chapter on the resurrection, Paul looks ahead to the day when death itself is swallowed up in victory.
1CO.15.26: Explaining the resurrection to the Corinthians, Paul says death is the last enemy that Christ will destroy.
2CO.1.20: Defending himself against accusations that he is unreliable, Paul says every one of God's promises is a 'yes' in Christ.
2CO.4.7: Paul describes the message of Jesus as a treasure carried in fragile clay jars, so that the power is clearly God's.
2CO.5.1: Worn down by hardship, Paul compares the human body to a tent that will one day be replaced by a permanent home from God.
2CO.5.21: Paul summarizes the heart of the gospel: the sinless Christ took on sin so that people could be made right with God.
2CO.9.15: At the end of a section about giving money generously, Paul bursts out in thanks for God's gift that is beyond words.
GAL.1.10: Defending his message to the Galatian churches, Paul says he is not trying to win people's approval, but God's.
GAL.6.10: Closing his letter to the Galatians, Paul urges them to do good to everyone whenever they have the chance.
EPH.2.13: Paul reminds non-Jewish believers in Ephesus that they were once far from God but have been brought near through Christ.
EPH.3.12: Paul tells the Ephesians that through faith in Christ they can approach God boldly and with confidence.
EPH.5.2: Paul urges the Ephesians to live a life of love, following the example of Christ, who gave himself for them.
EPH.5.20: In a passage about being filled with the Spirit, Paul encourages the Ephesians to always give thanks to God for everything.
PHP.1.3: Writing from prison, Paul opens his letter by telling the Philippian church that he thanks God every time he thinks of them.
PHP.2.4: Paul urges the Philippians to look out not only for their own interests, but for the interests of others.
PHP.4.12: Thanking the Philippians for a gift, Paul says he has learned how to be content whether he has plenty or very little.
COL.1.16: In a hymn-like passage about Christ, Paul tells the Colossians that everything in heaven and earth was created through him and for him.
COL.3.12: Paul tells the Colossians that as God's chosen and loved people, they should clothe themselves with compassion and kindness.
COL.3.16: Paul encourages the Colossians to let Christ's words fill their gatherings as they teach one another and sing with thankful hearts.
1TH.5.14: Near the end of his letter, Paul gives the Thessalonians practical ways to care for those who are struggling.
1TH.5.23: Paul closes his first letter to the Thessalonians with a prayer that the God of peace would make them whole.
1TI.1.16: Calling himself the worst of sinners, Paul tells Timothy that God showed him mercy as an example of Christ's patience.
1TI.6.17: Paul tells Timothy to instruct wealthy believers not to put their hope in money, but in God who provides everything.
2TI.1.9: Writing to Timothy from prison, Paul reminds him that God called them not because of what they did, but by his own grace.
2TI.2.13: Encouraging Timothy to endure hardship, Paul quotes what seems to be an early saying: even when we are faithless, God stays faithful.
2TI.4.18: In what is likely his last letter, written while awaiting execution, Paul says God will bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom.
TIT.2.11: Writing to Titus about how believers should live, Paul says God's grace has appeared and offers salvation to everyone.
HEB.2.18: The writer of Hebrews explains that because Jesus himself suffered temptation, he is able to help those who are being tempted.
HEB.7.25: The writer of Hebrews says Jesus is able to save completely because he always lives to speak to God on his people's behalf.
HEB.8.12: Quoting God's promise of a new covenant from Jeremiah, the writer of Hebrews says God will remember sins no more.
HEB.10.22: The writer of Hebrews invites readers to come near to God with confidence, their guilty consciences washed clean.
HEB.12.3: Encouraging readers who are growing weary, the writer of Hebrews tells them to think about everything Jesus endured.
HEB.12.12: After explaining that God's discipline is a sign of his love, the writer of Hebrews tells tired readers to strengthen their weak knees.
HEB.12.28: The writer of Hebrews says that because believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, they should be thankful.
JAS.1.3: Writing to scattered believers facing trials, James says that tested faith produces endurance.
JAS.1.4: James encourages his readers to let endurance finish its work, so they will be mature and lacking nothing.
JAS.1.22: James warns his readers that simply hearing God's word is not enough; they need to do what it says.
JAS.2.13: Warning against favoritism and harsh judgment, James says mercy wins out over judgment.
JAS.4.14: Addressing people who confidently plan their future, James reminds them that life is like a mist that quickly fades.
JAS.5.15: Encouraging the church to pray for the sick, James says a prayer offered in faith will raise them up.
1PE.2.10: Peter tells scattered believers that they were once not a people, but now they are God's people who have received mercy.
1PE.3.8: Peter gives the churches a summary of how to treat one another: with unity, sympathy, love, compassion and humility.
1PE.3.9: Peter tells believers facing hostility not to repay insult with insult, but to respond with blessing.
1PE.4.13: Writing to believers facing persecution, Peter tells them to rejoice that they share in Christ's sufferings.
2PE.1.3: Peter opens his second letter by saying God's power has already given believers everything they need for a godly life.
2PE.3.13: Responding to people who mock the idea of Christ's return, Peter says believers are waiting for a new heaven and earth.
1JN.2.1: Writing like a father to 'little children,' John says that when anyone does sin, Jesus speaks to the Father on their behalf.
1JN.2.12: John tells his readers he is writing to them because their sins have already been forgiven through Jesus' name.
1JN.3.16: John defines love by pointing to Jesus giving up his life, and says believers should do the same for one another.
1JN.4.7: John urges his readers to love one another, because love comes from God.
1JN.4.9: John says God's love was shown when he sent his only Son into the world so people could live through him.
1JN.4.10: John explains that real love is not about people loving God first, but about God loving them and sending his Son.
1JN.4.12: John notes that no one has ever seen God, but when people love one another, God lives in them.
1JN.4.16: John sums up what believers have come to know: God is love, and whoever lives in love lives in God.
1JN.5.13: Near the end of his letter, John says he wrote it so his readers could know for certain that they have eternal life.
REV.3.19: In a message to the lukewarm church in Laodicea, Jesus says he corrects those he loves and calls them to turn back.
REV.5.9: In John's vision of heaven, a new song is sung to the Lamb who was slain to rescue people from every nation.
REV.7.17: In John's vision, an elder describes people who came through great suffering, whom the Lamb will lead to living water.
REV.22.4: In the Bible's final vision of the new creation, John says God's people will finally see his face.
REV.22.20: In the last words of the Bible, Jesus promises he is coming soon, and John responds, 'Come, Lord Jesus.'
REV.21.3: In his vision of a new heaven and earth, John hears a voice announce that God will now live among his people.
REV.21.6: Speaking from the throne in John's vision, God declares 'It is done' and offers the water of life to the thirsty.
ISA.40.27: Speaking to exiles who feel God has lost track of them, Isaiah asks why they are saying their way is hidden from God.
ISA.49.14: Isaiah voices the complaint of Jerusalem, which feels forgotten by God, just before God answers with a promise.
JOB.23.3: Suffering and wanting answers, Job wishes he knew where to find God so he could bring his case before him.
PSA.44.23: After describing how his people have suffered despite staying loyal to God, the psalm's writer boldly asks why God seems asleep.
JHN.20.28: After doubting his friends' report, Thomas sees the risen Jesus and his wounds for himself and responds with this confession.
MAT.28.17: When the disciples meet the risen Jesus on a mountain in Galilee, Matthew honestly records that some of them still doubted.
GEN.15.8: After God promises Abram a land and countless descendants, Abram asks how he can be sure it will happen.
EXO.4.10: When God calls Moses to confront Pharaoh, Moses objects that he has never been a good speaker.
PSA.77.7: Unable to sleep, Asaph openly wonders whether God has rejected him forever.
PSA.77.8: Asaph continues voicing his fears, asking whether God's love has disappeared and his promises have failed.
ECC.8.17: The Preacher admits that no one, not even the wisest person, can fully make sense of what God is doing under the sun.
JHN.20.25: Thomas, who missed Jesus' first appearance after the resurrection, tells the other disciples he won't believe without seeing the wounds.
MAT.6.25: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus begins his teaching on worry by telling the crowd not to be anxious about food or clothing.
MAT.10.19: Sending out his disciples, Jesus warns they will be arrested, but tells them not to worry about what to say.
1SA.22.23: After King Saul massacres the priests of Nob, David takes in Abiathar, the lone survivor, and promises to keep him safe.
PSA.27.3: David says that even if an army surrounds him or war breaks out against him, his heart will stay confident.
ISA.41.14: God addresses Israel through Isaiah as small and weak like a worm, and promises that he himself will help them.
GEN.50.17: After their father's death, Joseph's brothers send him a message begging forgiveness, and Joseph weeps when he hears it.
JHN.11.27: Grieving her brother Lazarus, Martha answers Jesus' question with a clear statement of what she believes about him.
MRK.4.38: Caught in a storm that is filling their boat with water, the disciples wake the sleeping Jesus and ask if he even cares.
PSA.89.46: After celebrating God's promises to David's family, Ethan sees the dynasty in ruins and asks God how long he will hide.
JOB.3.26: After losing his children, his wealth and his health, Job describes the restlessness and turmoil that have overtaken him.
JHN.14.5: When Jesus tells his disciples they know the way to where he is going, Thomas honestly says they don't.
LUK.1.18: When an angel tells the elderly priest Zechariah that he will have a son, Zechariah asks how he can be sure.
LUK.1.38: After the angel Gabriel explains how she will conceive Jesus, Mary accepts her calling as God's servant.
MAT.26.75: After denying three times that he knows Jesus, Peter hears the rooster crow, remembers Jesus' words and weeps bitterly.
2CO.2.7: Paul urges the Corinthian church to forgive and comfort a member they had disciplined, so he won't be overwhelmed by sorrow.
2CO.2.8: Continuing his plea for a disciplined church member, Paul asks the Corinthians to reaffirm their love for him.
PSA.32.2: David describes the happiness of a person whose sins God no longer counts against them.
PSA.103.9: Listing God's kindnesses, David says God will not keep accusing people or stay angry forever.
PSA.73.2: Asaph begins his psalm by admitting that he nearly lost his footing and his faith when he saw evil people prospering.
PSA.55.4: Betrayed by a close friend, David describes his heart pounding with anguish and fear of death.
PSA.37.8: In a psalm about not envying people who get ahead by doing wrong, David urges his readers to let go of anger and stop fretting.
2TH.3.5: Near the end of his second letter to the Thessalonians, Paul prays that the Lord would guide their hearts into God's love and Christ's endurance.
1PE.3.14: Writing to believers facing hostility for their faith, Peter says those who suffer for doing right are blessed and need not be shaken.
